On the discriminants of truncated logarithmic polynomials

John Cullinan and Rylan Gajek-Leonard Address: Department of Mathematics, Bard College, Annandale-On-Hudson, NY 12504, USA Email address: cullinan@bard.edu URL: http://faculty.bard.edu/cullinan/ Address: Department of Mathematics, Union College, Schenectady, NY 12308, USA Email address: gajekler@union.edu URL: https://www.math.union.edu/~gajekler/
Abstract.

We provide evidence for a conjecture of Yamamura that the truncated logarithmic polynomials

Fn​(x)=1+x+x22+⋯+xnnF_{n}(x)=1+x+\frac{x^{2}}{2}+\cdots+\frac{x^{n}}{n}

have Galois group SnS_{n} for all n≥1n\geq 1.

1. Introduction

In [12], the authors consider two families of polynomials:

Fn​(x)\displaystyle F_{n}(x) =1+x+x22+⋯+xnn, and\displaystyle=1+x+\frac{x^{2}}{2}+\cdots+\frac{x^{n}}{n},\text{ and}
fn​(x)\displaystyle f_{n}(x) =1−x22!+⋯+(−1)n​x2​n(2​n)!.\displaystyle=1-\frac{x^{2}}{2!}+\cdots+\frac{(-1)^{n}x^{2n}}{(2n)!}.

These are the truncated Maclaurin polynomials of the functions F⁡(x)=1−log⁡(1−x)F(x)=1-\log(1-x) and f⁡(x)=cos⁡(x)f(x)=\cos(x), respectively. Motivated by Schur’s pioneering result on the truncated exponential polynomials [11], they work through the irreducibility and Galois groups of these polynomials. In the case of FnF_{n}, they prove that Gal𝐐⁡(Fn)\operatorname{Gal}_{\mathbf{Q}}(F_{n}) contains AnA_{n} for all nn.

However, their claim that Gal𝐐⁡(Fn)≃Sn\operatorname{Gal}_{\mathbf{Q}}(F_{n})\simeq S_{n} “depending on the residue of the integer number nn modulo 4” appears to be incorrect, as pointed out by Yamamura in his review of the paper for MathSciNet [13]. In fact, Yamamura therein conjectures that Gal𝐐⁡(Fn)≃Sn\operatorname{Gal}_{\mathbf{Q}}(F_{n})\simeq S_{n} for all n≥1n\geq 1. The purpose of this note is to address this conjecture and highlight the apparent difficulty of proving it in general.

By a Newton polygon argument in [12], the FnF_{n} are irreducible over 𝐐\mathbf{Q} with Gal𝐐⁡(Fn)⊇An\operatorname{Gal}_{\mathbf{Q}}(F_{n})\supseteq A_{n} for all n≥1n\geq 1. Thus, Yamamura’s conjecture amounts to proving that the discriminant of FnF_{n} is not a rational square once n>1n>1. Let us now set some notation.

The discriminant of a univariate polynomial P⁡(x)P(x) of degree nn and leading coefficient ana_{n} is given by

(1) disc⁡P=(−1)(n2)​an−1​Res⁡(P,P′).\displaystyle\operatorname{disc}P=(-1)^{\binom{n}{2}}a_{n}^{-1}\operatorname{Res}(P,P^{\prime}).

Computing the derivative

Fn′​(x)=1+x+x2+⋯+xn−1,F_{n}^{\prime}(x)=1+x+x^{2}+\cdots+x^{n-1},

whose roots are the nontrivial nn-th roots of unity, the discriminant we seek is therefore

(2) disc(Fn)=(−1)(n2)n∏{θ:Fn′​(θ)=0}Fn(θ).\displaystyle\operatorname{disc}(F_{n})=(-1)^{\binom{n}{2}}n\prod_{\{\theta:F_{n}^{\prime}(\theta)=0\}}F_{n}(\theta).

Let Ln=lcm⁡{1,2,…,n}L_{n}=\operatorname{lcm}\{1,2,\dots,n\}. Then

Fn​(x)=F~n​(x)Ln,F_{n}(x)=\frac{\widetilde{F}_{n}(x)}{L_{n}},

where F~n​(x)\widetilde{F}_{n}(x) is a polynomial with integer coefficients. The relations

θn=1and1+θ+θ2+⋯+θn−1=0\theta^{n}=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad 1+\theta+\theta^{2}+\cdots+\theta^{n-1}=0

hold when θ\theta is an nn-th root of unity, which allow us to simplify F~n​(θ)\widetilde{F}_{n}(\theta); we have

(3) F~n​(θ)=∑k=0n−2ak​θkwhereak={Ln+Lnn−Lnn−1if k=0Lnk−Lnn−1if k>0.\displaystyle\widetilde{F}_{n}(\theta)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}a_{k}\theta^{k}\qquad\text{where}\qquad a_{k}=\begin{cases}L_{n}+\frac{L_{n}}{n}-\frac{L_{n}}{n-1}&\text{if $k=0$}\\ \frac{L_{n}}{k}-\frac{L_{n}}{n-1}&\text{if $k>0$}.\end{cases}

Substituting (3) into (2) and simplifying yields the following expression for the discriminant of Fn​(x)F_{n}(x):

(4) disc(Fn)=(−1)(n2)nLnn−1∏{θ:Fn′​(θ)=0}F~n(θ).\displaystyle\operatorname{disc}(F_{n})=(-1)^{\binom{n}{2}}\frac{n}{L_{n}^{n-1}}\prod_{\{\theta:F_{n}^{\prime}(\theta)=0\}}\widetilde{F}_{n}(\theta).

Note that the product

(5) 𝒫n:⁣=∏{θ:Fn′​(θ)=0}F~n(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{n}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\prod_{\{\theta:F_{n}^{\prime}(\theta)=0\}}\widetilde{F}_{n}(\theta)

is an integer. As we will see below, the main difficulty in proving Yamamura’s conjecture is understanding the prime factorization of 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n}. We pause for an illustrative example.

Example 6.

Let n=9n=9. Then we compute

disc⁡(F9)\displaystyle\operatorname{disc}(F_{9}) =9L98∏{θ:F9′​(θ)=0}F~9(θ)=(3212​38​54​74)2𝒫9,\displaystyle=\frac{9}{L_{9}^{8}}\prod_{\{\theta:F_{9}^{\prime}(\theta)=0\}}\widetilde{F}_{9}(\theta)=\left(\frac{3}{2^{12}3^{8}5^{4}7^{4}}\right)^{2}\mathcal{P}_{9},

hence disc⁡(F9)\operatorname{disc}(F_{9}) is a rational square if and only if 𝒫9\mathcal{P}_{9} is. In this case, we compute

𝒫9=1531⋅3137311⋅113564970051005791,\mathcal{P}_{9}=1531\cdot 3137311\cdot 113564970051005791,

and these prime factors do not appear to be predictable a priori.

The above example illustrates the main difficulty in proving disc⁡(Fn)∉𝐐×2\operatorname{disc}(F_{n})\not\in\mathbf{Q}^{\times 2} when nn is a square: the factor 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} is typically not divisible by primes dividing nn, so we cannot use “small” primes to our advantage. And, additionally, the prime divisors of 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} may be quite difficult or impossible to characterize.

In [12] the authors show that if n≡0,2,3(mod4)n\equiv 0,2,3\pmod{4}, then disc⁡(Fn)∉𝐐×2\operatorname{disc}(F_{n})\not\in\mathbf{Q}^{\times 2}. They then prove that if n≡1(mod4)n\equiv 1\pmod{4} and nn is prime, then disc⁡(Fn)∉𝐐×2\operatorname{disc}(F_{n})\not\in\mathbf{Q}^{\times 2}. In some cases, our results can be viewed as a companion to theirs: we were unable to easily verify some of their claims, and so we give independent proofs of these discriminant results, as well as some mild generalizations.

Theorem 7.

If n≡0,2,3(mod4)n\equiv 0,2,3\pmod{4}, or if n≡1(mod4)n\equiv 1\pmod{4} and is the odd power of a prime, then disc⁡(Fn)∉𝐐×2\operatorname{disc}(F_{n})\not\in\mathbf{Q}^{\times 2}.

Regarding the prime divisors of 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n}, we can say the following as a generalization of Example 6.

Theorem 8.

If n=p2​en=p^{2e} for an odd prime pp and a positive integer ee, then 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} is coprime to pp.

However, the main contribution of this paper is to give substantially new infinite families of integers n≡1(mod4)n\equiv 1\pmod{4} for which disc⁡(Fn)\operatorname{disc}(F_{n}) is not a rational square.

Theorem 9.

Let mm be a positive integer. For all but finitely many primes qq, if m​q≡1(mod4)mq\equiv 1\pmod{4} then disc⁡(Fm​q)∉𝐐×2\operatorname{disc}(F_{mq})\not\in\mathbf{Q}^{\times 2}.

Remark 10.

For each integer mm one can explicitly compute the finite set of primes for which the above theorem does not apply. It is then a matter of computation to check that disc⁡(Fn)∉𝐐×2\operatorname{disc}(F_{n})\not\in\mathbf{Q}^{\times 2} for each of these exceptional primes. We give examples to demonstrate this in the final section of this article.

Before proving our results, we briefly survey the calculation of discriminants for number-theoretic purposes.

2. Commentary on Discriminants, Resultants, and Arithmetic

The systematic study of the algebraic properties of families of orthogonal polynomials appears to originate in two papers of Holt [6, 7], in which he studies the irreducibility of certain Legendre polynomials. Holt’s methods were generalized significantly by Ille and Schur [11], leading to extensive studies of the irreducibility and Galois theory of many families of hypergeometric polynomials (e.g., Jacobi, Laguerre, Chebyshev, Hermite). Assuming irreducibility, there are Newton Polygon methods that will allow one to prove that the Galois group contains AnA_{n}. Deciding whether or not the Galois group is all of SnS_{n} is then a matter of determining when the discriminant is a rational square.

The applications of orthogonal polynomials to arithmetic go beyond computational Galois theory. In particular, if ssp​(t)∈𝐅p​[t]{\rm ss}_{p}(t)\in\mathbf{F}_{p}[t] denotes the supersingular polynomial (whose roots are the supersingular jj-invariants of elliptic curves over 𝐅p\mathbf{F}_{p}), then ssp​(t){\rm ss}_{p}(t) is the reduction modulo pp of a certain Jacobi polynomial. For more background and for other interesting lifts of ssp​(t){\rm ss}_{p}(t) to 𝐐\mathbf{Q}, see [8, 10]. A conjecture of Mahburg and Ono [9] states that the “Jacobi lifts” are irreducible with maximal Galois group, and in [5] we gave evidence for this conjecture using many of the techniques originally described by Schur.

In the case of the classical families of orthogonal polynomials, the discriminants tend to have nice expressions. A prototypical example is the case of the truncated exponential polynomials

en​(x)=∑j=0nxjj!,e_{n}(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\frac{x^{j}}{j!},

whose discriminants are given by disc⁡(en)=(−1)(n2)​(n!)n\operatorname{disc}(e_{n})=\left(-1\right)^{\binom{n}{2}}\left(n!\right)^{n}. This formula is a key feature of Coleman’s proof that Gal𝐐⁡(en)\operatorname{Gal}_{\mathbf{Q}}\left(e_{n}\right) always contains AnA_{n} and equals SnS_{n} if and only if 4∤n4\nmid n [2]. We note that if

Ln(α)​(x)=∑i=0n(−1)i​(n+αn−i)​xii!{\displaystyle L_{n}^{(\alpha)}(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}(-1)^{i}{n+\alpha\choose n-i}{\frac{x^{i}}{i!}}}

denotes the nnth Generalized Laguerre Polynomial (GLP), then en​(x)=Ln(−1−n)​(x)e_{n}(x)=L_{n}^{(-1-n)}(x).

Ultimately, the reason that certain hypergeometric polynomials (including all of the ones mentioned above) have such tidy discriminant formulas is that they satisfy a Sturm-Liouville differential equation, relating the derivative of a member of the family to another member, and that the polynomials solve certain recurrence relations; for example, in the case of the GLP we have

dd​x​Ln(α)​(x)=−Ln−1(α+1)​(x).\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}x}L_{n}^{(\alpha)}(x)=-L_{n-1}^{(\alpha+1)}(x).

The recurrence relations, together with the differential equations, typically allow for explicit discriminant formulas, via (1), which are amenable to arithmetic study.

This is not the case with the truncated logarithmic polynomials Fn​(x)F_{n}(x) – the derivative of Fn​(x)F_{n}(x) does not belong to the same family (as in the case of the classical orthogonal polynomials). However, the roots of Fn′​(x)F^{\prime}_{n}(x) are the nontrivial nn-th roots of unity, hence are independently equipped with a good deal of algebraic and arithmetic symmetry. Thus, from the point of view of discriminants, our family {Fn​(x)}\{F_{n}(x)\} is more amenable to computation than a “random” family of polynomials, but is harder to work with than a family of classical orthogonal polynomials. This manifests itself in (4) where we understand some of the prime factorization quite well (viz., n/Lnn−1n/L_{n}^{n-1}) and the rest (𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n}) not at all.

3. Preliminary Results

We start with a concise proof that disc⁡(Fn)∉𝐐×2\operatorname{disc}(F_{n})\not\in\mathbf{Q}^{\times 2} when n≢1(mod4)n\not\equiv 1\pmod{4}.

Proposition 11.

If n≡0,2,or ​3(mod4)n\equiv 0,2,\text{or }3\pmod{4}, then disc⁡(Fn)∉𝐐×2\operatorname{disc}(F_{n})\not\in\mathbf{Q}^{\times 2}.

Proof.

If n≡2,3(mod4)n\equiv 2,3\pmod{4} then disc⁡(Fn)<0\operatorname{disc}(F_{n})<0, by (2). For n≡0(mod4)n\equiv 0\pmod{4}, we first compute disc⁡(F4)=725/432∉𝐐×2\operatorname{disc}(F_{4})=725/432\not\in\mathbf{Q}^{\times 2}. If n≥8n\geq 8, then there exists a prime number in the interval (n/2,n−2)(n/2,n-2). Fix such a prime ℓ\ell and observe that vℓ​(n)=0v_{\ell}(n)=0 and that vℓ​(Ln)=1v_{\ell}(L_{n})=1. Thus vℓ​(n/Lnn−1)v_{\ell}\left(n/L_{n}^{n-1}\right) is odd. For a nontrivial nn-th root of unity θ\theta, consider F~n​(θ)\widetilde{F}_{n}(\theta). Reducing (3) modulo ℓ\ell, we have F~n​(θ)≡(Ln/ℓ)​θℓ(modℓ)\widetilde{F}_{n}(\theta)\equiv\left(L_{n}/\ell\right)\theta^{\ell}\pmod{\ell}, whence 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} is coprime to ℓ\ell:

𝒫n=∏{θ:Fn′​(θ)=0}F~n(θ)≡∏{θ:Fn′​(θ)=0}Lnℓθℓ(modℓ)≡(Lnℓ)n−1⋅(−1)≢0(modℓ).\mathcal{P}_{n}=\prod_{\{\theta:F_{n}^{\prime}(\theta)=0\}}\widetilde{F}_{n}(\theta)\equiv\prod_{\{\theta:F_{n}^{\prime}(\theta)=0\}}\frac{L_{n}}{\ell}\theta^{\ell}\pmod{\ell}\equiv\left(\frac{L_{n}}{\ell}\right)^{n-1}\cdot(-1)\not\equiv 0\pmod{\ell}.

Thus vℓ​(disc⁡(Fn))v_{\ell}(\operatorname{disc}(F_{n})) is odd and so disc⁡(Fn)∉𝐐×2\operatorname{disc}(F_{n})\not\in\mathbf{Q}^{\times 2}. ∎

This brings us to the case n≡1(mod4)n\equiv 1\pmod{4}, which is the most mysterious. We start by generalizing [12, Thm. 3.1] to when nn is a prime power.

Theorem 12.

Let p≡1(mod4)p\equiv 1\pmod{4}, ee a positive integer, and n=pen=p^{e}. Then 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} is coprime to pp.

Proof.

We start by reducing the factors F~n​(θ)\widetilde{F}_{n}(\theta) of 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} modulo pp:

a0\displaystyle a_{0} =Ln+Lnn−Lnn−1≡Lnn(modp)≢0(modp), and\displaystyle=L_{n}+\frac{L_{n}}{n}-\frac{L_{n}}{n-1}\equiv\frac{L_{n}}{n}\pmod{p}\not\equiv 0\pmod{p},\text{ and}
ak\displaystyle a_{k} =Lnk−Lnn−1≡0(modp)\displaystyle=\frac{L_{n}}{k}-\frac{L_{n}}{n-1}\equiv 0\pmod{p}

for all k=1,…​n−2k=1,\dots n-2, due to the fact that 0≤vp​(k)≤e−10\leq v_{p}(k)\leq e-1 for all such kk. Therefore

𝒫n=∏{θ:Fn′​(θ)=0}F~n(θ)≡∏{θ:Fn′​(θ)=0}Lnn≡(Lnn)n−1≢0(modp),\mathcal{P}_{n}=\prod_{\{\theta:F_{n}^{\prime}(\theta)=0\}}\widetilde{F}_{n}(\theta)\equiv\prod_{\{\theta:F_{n}^{\prime}(\theta)=0\}}\frac{L_{n}}{n}\equiv\left(\frac{L_{n}}{n}\right)^{n-1}\not\equiv 0\pmod{p},

as claimed. ∎

Corollary 13.

Let p≡1(mod4)p\equiv 1\pmod{4}, ee a positive integer, and n=pen=p^{e}. If ee is odd, then disc⁡(Fn)∉𝐐×2\operatorname{disc}(F_{n})\not\in\mathbf{Q}^{\times 2}. If ee is even, then disc⁡(Fn)∉𝐐×2\operatorname{disc}(F_{n})\not\in\mathbf{Q}^{\times 2} if and only if 𝒫n∉𝐐×2\mathcal{P}_{n}\not\in\mathbf{Q}^{\times 2}.

Proof.

Note that whether ee is even or odd, we have

vp​(disc⁡(Fn))=vp​(n)−(n−1)​vp​(Ln)+vp​(𝒫n)=e−e⁡(n−1)+0,v_{p}\left(\operatorname{disc}(F_{n})\right)=v_{p}(n)-(n-1)v_{p}(L_{n})+v_{p}(\mathcal{P}_{n})=e-e(n-1)+0,

by Theorem 12. If ee is odd, then vp​(disc⁡(Fn))v_{p}\left(\operatorname{disc}(F_{n})\right) is odd (because n≡1(mod4)n\equiv 1\pmod{4}) and hence disc⁡(Fn)∉𝐐×2\operatorname{disc}(F_{n})\not\in\mathbf{Q}^{\times 2}. If ee is even, then n/Lnn−1n/L_{n}^{n-1} is a rational square, hence disc⁡(Fn)\operatorname{disc}(F_{n}) is a rational square if and only if 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} is. ∎

By Example 6, we cannot expect to make much general progress on the case when n≡1(mod4)n\equiv 1\pmod{4} when nn is a square, due to the unpredictable prime factorization of 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n}. For the rest of the paper, we assume n≡1(mod4)n\equiv 1\pmod{4} is not a square.

4. The Case n=m​qn=mq

Fix a positive integer mm, let ω\omega be a primitive mmth root of unity, and define

X⁡(m)\displaystyle X(m) :⁣=∏k=1m−11m+ωk+12ω2​k+⋯+1(m−1)ω(m−1)​k\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\prod_{k=1}^{m-1}\frac{1}{m}+\omega^{k}+\frac{1}{2}\omega^{2k}+\cdots+\frac{1}{(m-1)}\omega^{(m-1)k}
Y⁡(m)\displaystyle Y(m) :⁣=1+12+⋯+1m.\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}1+\frac{1}{2}+\cdots+\frac{1}{m}.

Observe that both X⁡(m)X(m) and Y⁡(m)Y(m) are rational numbers. Consider the set

Em={primes ℓ∣vℓ​(X​(m))>0, vℓ​(Y​(m))>0, and m​ℓ≡1(mod4)}{\rm E}_{m}=\{\text{primes $\ell$}\mid\text{$v_{\ell}(X(m))>0$, $v_{\ell}(Y(m))>0$, and $m\ell\equiv 1\pmod{4}$}\}

consisting of all prime divisors of X⁡(m)X(m) and Y⁡(m)Y(m) whose product with mm is congruent to 1(mod4)1\pmod{4}.

Remark 14.

While Em{\rm E}_{m} can be computed explicitly for fixed mm, we expect that saying anything in general about this set could be difficult. Even without considering X⁡(m)X(m), the set Em{\rm E}_{m} relies on understanding pp-adic properties of the sequence Y⁡(m)Y(m) of harmonic numbers, which is known to be a hard problem (see [1]).

Theorem 15.

For all primes qq such that q∉Emq\not\in{\rm E}_{m}, gcd⁡(q,m)=1\gcd(q,m)=1, and n:⁣=mq≡1(mod4)n\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}mq\equiv 1\pmod{4}, we have disc⁡(Fn)∉𝐐×2\operatorname{disc}(F_{n})\not\in\mathbf{Q}^{\times 2}.

Proof.

Recall that

(16) disc⁡(Fm​q)=m​qLm​qm​q−1​𝒫m​q.\operatorname{disc}(F_{mq})=\frac{mq}{L_{mq}^{mq-1}}\mathcal{P}_{mq}.

Since m​q≡1(mod4)mq\equiv 1\pmod{4}, we have that vq​(m​qLm​qm​q−1)v_{q}\left(\frac{mq}{L_{mq}^{mq-1}}\right) is odd. Thus, if vq​(𝒫m​q)v_{q}(\mathcal{P}_{mq}) is even, then disc⁡(Fm​q)∉𝐐×2\operatorname{disc}(F_{mq})\not\in\mathbf{Q}^{\times 2}. We now compute 𝒫m​q(modq)\mathcal{P}_{mq}\pmod{q}.

Let θk=exp⁡(2​π​i/m​q)k\theta_{k}=\exp(2\pi i/mq)^{k} and ω=exp⁡(2​π​i/m)\omega=\exp(2\pi i/m). Then

𝒫m​q=∏k=1m​q−1(∑j=0m​q−2aj​θkj).\mathcal{P}_{mq}=\prod_{k=1}^{mq-1}\left(\sum_{j=0}^{mq-2}a_{j}\theta_{k}^{j}\right).

Reducing each coefficient modulo qq gives us

𝒫m​q\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{mq} ≡∏k=1m​q−1(a0+aq​θkq+a2​q​θk2​q+⋯+a(m−1)​q​θk(m−1)​q)(modq)\displaystyle\equiv\prod_{k=1}^{mq-1}\left(a_{0}+a_{q}\theta_{k}^{q}+a_{2q}\theta_{k}^{2q}+\cdots+a_{(m-1)q}\theta_{k}^{(m-1)q}\right)\pmod{q}
≡∏k=1m​q−1(a0+aq​ωk+a2​q​ω2​k+⋯+a(m−1)​q​ωk⁡(m−1))(modq)\displaystyle\equiv\prod_{k=1}^{mq-1}\left(a_{0}+a_{q}\omega^{k}+a_{2q}\omega^{2k}+\cdots+a_{(m-1)q}\omega^{k(m-1)}\right)\pmod{q}
≡∏k=1m​q−1(Lm​qm​q+Lm​qq​ωk+Lm​q2​q​ω2​k+⋯+Lm​q(m−1)​q​ωk⁡(m−1))(modq)\displaystyle\equiv\prod_{k=1}^{mq-1}\left(\frac{L_{mq}}{mq}+\frac{L_{mq}}{q}\omega^{k}+\frac{L_{mq}}{2q}\omega^{2k}+\cdots+\frac{L_{mq}}{(m-1)q}\omega^{k(m-1)}\right)\pmod{q}

5. Examples and Conclusions

We conclude the paper with several examples and observations. We start by setting m=pm=p a prime number in Theorem 15. If we fix pp, then as long as both X⁡(p)X(p) and Y⁡(p)Y(p) are coprime to q>pq>p, we can conclude that disc⁡(Fp​q)∉𝐐×2\operatorname{disc}(F_{pq})\not\in\mathbf{Q}^{\times 2}. For the remaining values of q∈Epq\in{\rm E}_{p}, we can check by hand as long as it is computationally feasible. The following result is a sample implementation of our methods. We note that other examples with n=p​qn=pq are similarly easy to generate.

Proposition 17.

For any prime qq, if n=3​qn=3q, 5​q5q, or 7​q7q, then disc⁡(Fn)∉𝐐×2\operatorname{disc}(F_{n})\not\in\mathbf{Q}^{\times 2}.

Proof.

If n≡2,3(mod4)n\equiv 2,3\pmod{4}, we are done by Proposition 11. We have seen in Example 6 that disc⁡(F9)∉𝐐×2\operatorname{disc}(F_{9})\not\in\mathbf{Q}^{\times 2}. By using the issquare command in PariGP we check that neither disc⁡(F25)\operatorname{disc}(F_{25}) nor disc⁡(F49)\operatorname{disc}(F_{49}) is a rational square.

It therefore suffices to consider n=3​qn=3q, 5​q5q, or 7​q7q in the case n≡1(mod4)n\equiv 1\pmod{4} and q>3,5,7q>3,5,7, respectively. By Theorem 15, we are reduced to checking finitely many cases. We close with several observations which suggest that a different approach than that discussed in this paper may be necessary in order to prove Yamamura’s conjecture in general. In particular, the condition that n=m​qn=mq with q>mq>m and gcd⁡(m,q)=1\gcd(m,q)=1 is a strong hypothesis that we cannot remove. What cases are left to prove? Among all n≡1(mod4)n\equiv 1\pmod{4}, either

  • •

    nn is an odd square, or

  • •

    nn has at least two distinct prime divisors, and at least one prime divisor at which nn has odd valuation.

In the second case, Theorem 15 handles values of the form

n=q1e1q2e2⋯qr−1er−1qr,n=q_{1}^{e_{1}}q_{2}^{e_{2}}\cdots q_{r-1}^{e_{r}-1}q_{r},

for prime numbers q1<q2<⋯qrq_{1}<q_{2}<\cdots q_{r}. With regard to generalizing the proof of Theorem 15, we present the following data as evidence that a different approach is needed.

  1. (1)

    The condition q>mq>m in Theorem 15 allows us to compute F~m​q​(θ)(modq)\widetilde{F}_{mq}(\theta)\pmod{q} easily – the only aka_{k} which are not divisible by qq are the aj​qa_{jq} for j=1,…,m−1j=1,\dots,m-1. If q<mq<m, then we would need to include additional multiples of qq less than mm.
